analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate prescription drug prices directly with drug manufacturers.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 45 cosponsors including one Republican, never received a committee or floor vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law explicitly forbids the government from negotiating Medicare drug prices with pharmaceutical companies. This bill deletes that ban and requires the Health and Human Services Secretary to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates for the drugs covered under Medicare's prescription drug benefit, starting with 2018 plan years. The bill also requires the Secretary to report to Congress every six months on the price reductions achieved.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 40 million Medicare beneficiaries who pay for prescription drugs, plus taxpayers, since Medicare covers a large share of those prices. Lower negotiated prices would reduce out-of-pocket costs for beneficiaries and reduce federal drug spending.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the statutory 'non-interference' provision that prohibits the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating covered Part D drug prices, and replaces it with a requirement to negotiate prices, discounts, and rebates with manufacturers on behalf of Medicare beneficiaries [S2] [S3].

Preserves plans' ability to obtain even deeper discounts than the Secretary negotiates, and does not authorize the Secretary to mandate a particular formulary, so beneficiaries' access rules are unchanged [S3].
Requires semi-annual reports to four congressional committees on the negotiations conducted and the prices and discounts achieved, creating public accountability for the results [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, whose revenue on Medicare-covered drugs would be reduced by negotiated discounts and rebates. Insurers offering Medicare drug plans could see narrower margins if negotiated prices compress the rebates that help fund plan benefits.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not specify any price target, benchmark, or enforcement mechanism; negotiation outcomes would depend entirely on the Secretary's leverage, which is uncertain because the bill keeps the Part D program's private-insurer structure intact [S3].

The pharmaceutical industry's standard objection, outside the record of this bill, is that government price negotiation would reduce manufacturers' revenues and could slow investment in new drugs; an honest supporter would acknowledge the tension between lower prices today and research incentives over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is concrete: Medicare is one of the largest drug buyers in the world, and other large purchasers negotiate while the government is barred from doing so, which requires taxpayer and beneficiary money to be spent on manufacturers' terms [S2] [S3]. The bill is modest in design — it relies on negotiation rather than price caps, keeps private drug plans in place, and does not define price targets — so its real-world savings would depend on execution. The main cost falls on drug makers' Medicare revenue and, potentially, on the pace of new drug development, a tradeoff supporters consider worth making.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and to their health subcommittees, and it sat there for the entire two years of the Congress without a markup, a vote, or ever reaching the floor.

narrative.text: Representative Peter Welch introduced the bill on January 4, 2017, the opening day of the 115th Congress, joined by 15 original cosponsors [S3].
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the House Ways and Means Committee, and within weeks both referred it to their Health subcommittees [S5].

It attracted 45 cosponsors — 44 Democrats and 1 Republican — but no committee ever reported it out, and the action history shows no further activity after the January 2017 subcommittee referrals [S4] [S5].
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without any vote in either chamber [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers and the existing Part D arrangement, in which the government is legally barred from negotiating and drug prices are set on manufacturers' terms, were better off because the bill never advanced. Medicare beneficiaries and taxpayers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Democratic — 44 of the 45 cosponsors — with one Republican joining; the bill never reached a vote where a partisan breakdown would have been recorded [S4].

industries.note: The bill would end the legal ban on Medicare price negotiation and require manufacturers to accept negotiated prices, discounts, and rebates on drugs bought for tens of millions of beneficiaries [S2] [S3]. Because the bill died in committee, manufacturers kept the existing non-interference protection for the rest of the Congress.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and pharmacy benefit managers
industries.note: The bill leaves private drug plans and MA-PD plans in place and even lets them negotiate deeper discounts below the government-negotiated price, but centralized price negotiation would compress the manufacturer rebates that fund plan benefits [S3]. The industry's favored status quo — plans and PBMs operating on manufacturers' terms with no government negotiation — survived unchanged.
